content:
I discovered a feature hidden in the System Settings app on my Mac that I never knew existed: you can set different default languages for individual Mac apps. If you already know about this, there's nothing to see here—move along. Otherwise, here's how it works (and where it falls short)…

In real life, plenty of bilingual people have to switch between languages throughout their day, depending on who they're talking to or what they're doing. I don't have that problem, but I do frequently have to switch between British English (i.e. English…) and American English.

(Just to be clear, this is a friendly joke! Some British English spellings are actually holdovers from American English that later changed in Britain—like the -ize ending that became -ise in British English. As James Nicoll once put it: "The problem with defending the purity of the English language is that English is about as pure as a cribhouse whore. We don't just borrow words; on occasion, English has pursued other languages down alleyways to beat them unconscious and rifle their pockets for new vocabulary.")

Switching between the two varieties of English means I can't rely on spell-check to catch cases where I've used the right word but in the wrong flavour of English. I'd always assumed this was something I'd just have to deal with manually, but today I discovered there's at least a partial workaround.

Buried at the very bottom of System Settings > General > Language & Region is an "Applications" section. You can add apps here and then select a language. Apple's US-centric approach is on full display here: British English is labelled "English (UK)" while American English is called "English – English".

In my case, since I do most of my writing in a browser, I use two different browsers depending on the target language. I have British English set as my system language, so Safari uses British English; Chrome (listed alphabetically as Google Chrome) is set to American English.

However, there's one important limitation I've discovered: you can only do this for apps that support macOS's internationalisation/language APIs, so not every app shows up in the list.

If I'm the last person on Earth to discover this, feel free to give me your multilingual side-eye in the comments.
